The name of an object

Source: R/name.R
name.Rd

Many logmu objects can carry a name of their own: a mortality, a model(), an include or indicator and each term of a covariates(). name() reads it and name<- sets or, with NULL, clears it. Where an object has one, the name is what logmu prints for it, so a reference mortality shows as S4PMA rather than as <mortality_table>, and a model handed to compare_models() without a list name is labelled by its own.

An include carries a second level, its group_name, which says which breakdown it belongs to: age for [60, 70). Over a whole includes() the two levels are read as vectors by names() and group_names().

Usage

name(x)

name(x) <- value

group_name(x)

group_name(x) <- value

Arguments

x

An object.

value

A name, or NULL to clear it.

Value

name() and group_name() return a single string, or NULL where the object has none.

name<- and group_name<- return x with the name set.

What a name may be

A name is a single string that is not blank, has no leading, trailing or consecutive spaces, and holds no control character such as a tab or a newline. The rule is the same for every name in the package, whether you wrote it or logmu generated it: [60, 70), >= 70 and a+b are all names it makes for itself, and they follow the rule too.

Examples

base <- mortality_const(log_mu = -4, name = "flat")
name(base)
#> [1] "flat"

m <- model(ref_mortality = base, covariates = covariates(level = 1))
name(m) <- "one level"
m
#> <model: 1 term>
#>   name:      one level
#>   reference: flat
#>   [1] level

std <- ages(65, 95, by = 15)
name(std[[1]])
#> [1] "65-80"
group_name(std[[1]])
#> [1] "age"
